Stage 3d: the labour block on the regional core

The rollout stage 3c said could not happen — and what a bloc changes about what a column of k buys

1. What this is, and why it exists

reports/stage3c_rollout.qmd set out to roll the stage-3 blocks across the euro area and concluded it could not be done:

Data availability is not the constraint. […] The constraint is the degrees-of-freedom budget, and it binds by roughly a factor of two: the system is already at df = 8 with one country carrying the blocks, and a second fully-loaded country would need k = 104 against T = 98.

That conclusion was right about the eleven-country partition and does not bind on the six-entity one. Stage 2d re-partitions the world — de, fr, it, us, cn and the reu bloc — and in doing so drops k from 76 to 46. The labour block still costs seven columns per entity; it is simply being added to a system with thirty columns of room instead of none.

But the arithmetic is not the interesting part. What a bloc changes is what a column buys. reu is one entity covering seven economies, so giving it the block extends the wage–price channel to seven countries for the price of one:

The affordability frontier on the regional core. Compare stage 3c’s, where DE+FR labour alone reached df = 8 and covered two economies.
Configuration Labour entities Economies covered k T df Feasible (df >= 4)
stage 2d (no labour block) 0 0 46 78 32 yes
de 1 1 53 78 25 yes
de + reu 2 8 60 78 18 yes
de + reu + fr 3 9 67 78 11 yes
de + reu + fr + it 4 10 74 78 4 yes

This report estimates the de + reu configuration: 8 of the eleven modelled economies carry a wage–price block, at df = 18, against stage 3a’s one economy at df = 15.

System Economies with the block Equations k T df
Stage 2d (core) 0 38 + 25 46 78 32
Stage 3a (DE on stage 2b) 1 74 + 39 83 98 15
Stage 3d (DE + REU on stage 2d) 8 50 + 33 60 78 18

Phase A only: <iso2>_foreign_prices stays exogenous. Stage 3a’s phase B — giving every partner an export-price equation so foreign prices become an identity — cost ten columns on eleven countries and would cost five here, but it is a separate question from the one this stage asks.

2. The bloc’s labour variables

reu_wages is the GDP-weighted average of seven national wage growth rates, not a euro-per-worker level, and reu_employment is an index rather than a headcount. That is the right object for a model estimated in growth space — every stage-3a identity is a statement about growth rates, and they reproduce on the bloc exactly as on a country — but the levels are not quotable.

HICP basket split. A bloc has no published basket, so bloc_hicp_weights() averages its members’ with the same weights the bloc’s series were built from; the members are shown indented.
entity nonenergy energy
DE 0.8875 0.1125
REU 0.9006 0.0994
AT 0.9159 0.0841
BE 0.8939 0.1061
ES 0.8918 0.1082
GR 0.9173 0.0827
IE 0.9054 0.0946
NL 0.9019 0.0981
PT 0.9101 0.0899

The bloc’s energy share (9.9%) sits inside its members’ range and just below Germany’s (11.3%). The weights are renormalised to sum to exactly 1, which labour_block() requires: the split partitions the basket, and seven rounded weights can otherwise leave a 1e-4 residual that would abort the block for no real reason.

The foreign-price index is better here than in stage 3a

foreign_price_weights(): the trade-weighted index each entity’s export and import prices load on.
Entity Partner weights (renormalised) row_gdp weight dropped
DE fr 0.119, it 0.096, us 0.180, cn 0.191, reu 0.414 0.456
REU de 0.315, fr 0.175, it 0.114, us 0.210, cn 0.186 0.458

There is no rest-of-world export-price series, so the row_gdp residual is dropped and the remainder renormalised — the index therefore assumes the unmodelled world prices like the modelled partners. In stage 3a that reallocated 0.572 of German trade; here it reallocates 0.456. The improvement is not a modelling choice, it is coverage: the US and China are now partners with export-price series of their own (FRED’s implicit deflator and IMF IFS PXP_IX), so a fifth of German trade that stage 3a had to assume away is now observed.

NoteA bug this stage exposed

reu_prices initially failed the exact-identity check by 1.47e-07 — small, but the identity is supposed to be exact. The cause was in identity_equation(), which rendered weights with format()’s default 7 significant digits while the identity’s left-hand side series is built from the full-precision numeric weight. Every weight in the project until now was a rounded expenditure or trade share, so the two always agreed; the bloc’s HICP split is a seven-member average and is not a round number. koma has no identity-consistency check, so this would have been enforced in silence. Fixed by rendering 15 digits, which leaves every already-rounded weight identical — verified against the cached stage-2b and 2c systems.

4. What the bloc identifies that Germany alone does not

Equation Entity Term Estimate 90% interval
Wage Phillips curve DE (stage 3a) de_unemployment -0.136 [-0.327, 0.038]
DE / REU (stage 3d) de_unemployment / reu_unemployment -0.105 / -0.176 [-0.278, 0.057] / [-0.301, -0.053]
Okun (employment) DE de_gdp 0.101 [0.060, 0.154]
REU reu_gdp 0.349 [0.288, 0.400]
Export-price pass-through DE de_foreign_prices 0.464 [0.256, 0.662]
REU reu_foreign_prices 0.909 [0.561, 1.250]

The wage Phillips curve is identified on the bloc and not on Germany. Germany’s wage–unemployment coefficient is -0.105 with an interval of [-0.278, 0.057] — correctly signed but straddling zero, which is also what stage 3a found on its own window. The bloc’s is -0.176, interval [-0.301, -0.053] — the interval excludes zero.

That is the aggregation working for identification rather than against it, and it is worth being precise about why. Germany’s unemployment rate moves in a narrow band over this window; the bloc’s is a GDP-weighted average that includes Spain, Greece and Ireland, whose unemployment rates swung by tens of percentage points across the sovereign-debt crisis. The bloc has far more variation in the regressor, and a wage equation can see the relationship through it. reu_employment’s Okun coefficient (0.349 against Germany’s 0.101) says the same thing from the other side: employment in the bloc is far more responsive to output than in Germany, which matches everything known about those labour markets.

This cuts the other way too, and the sign checks say where.

Two of the 6 are in the bloc’s own labour block and both are about pass-through, not about the cycle: reu_wages does not index to reu_prices (-0.067) and reu_export_prices does not load on reu_ulc (-0.076). Both are plausibly the aggregation: indexation arrangements and cost pass-through differ sharply across seven economies, so averaging their growth rates averages away the very mechanism the coefficient is trying to measure. The cyclical relationships — which depend on co-movement rather than on a shared institutional parameter — survive aggregation; the institutional ones do not.

That is a genuine limitation of the bloc, and it is the opposite trade to the one Germany makes: Germany has the institutions but not the variation.

NoteA second bug this stage exposed

sign_checks() reported phillips_curve_positive as a failure for both labour entities with estimate = NA. Under the labour block <iso2>_prices is an identity over the energy and non-energy sub-indices, so there is no prices ~ gdp coefficient to look at — the same claim is made and checked by price_phillips_curve_negative on nonenergy_prices. The stage-2c rule is now dropped for a labour country, exactly as the spread and financial rules already were. Two deliberate absences were being reported as failures.

All three policy rates reach every price variable in the system, including the disaggregated ones the labour block introduces. Stage 2c’s structural fix survives both the re-partition and the block.

One caveat the extension table makes visible. de_foreign_prices and reu_foreign_prices are extended by eight quarters, not three — the whole forecast window — because they are chained indices over partners’ export prices and stop where the shortest partner does, which is China’s IFS export-price index at 2024Q4. Their extrapolated path is flat (trailing-4Q average growth of 0.00%/q, export prices having been flat), so this is a conservative assumption rather than a wild one, but the price channel’s external driver is assumption rather than data across the whole horizon.

7. Verdict

Economies with a wage–price channel 8 of 11, against stage 3a’s 1
df 18, against stage 3a’s 15 and stage 3b’s 8
Acceptance tuning converges to 0 flagged equations
Explosive own lags none
Sign checks 56 of 62
Wage Phillips curve identified on the bloc, not on Germany
Wage indexation, ULC pass-through lost to aggregation on the bloc

Stage 3c’s finding was not wrong; it was partition-specific. “The rollout cannot happen” was a true statement about eleven countries and a false one about the world. What changed is not the estimator, the data or the block — it is that a bloc makes one column of k buy seven economies instead of one.

What this does not do. It does not give Spain or Greece their own wage equation — they have a share in one. An institution-specific question (national indexation, a country’s own ULC pass-through) still needs a country-level block, and stage 3c’s arithmetic still applies to that. The bloc answers regional questions: what a euro-area-wide wage–price spiral does to the core, and how the labour channel changes a spillover.
